finding: The brief change makes a driver-spawned unit's first command exit 2 for roles the driver itself chose to spawn. §4.2 changes UnitKind.BriefCommand to `tp review <spec> --role <id>` / `tp audit <spec> --role <id>`, and bullet 3 makes a name outside the emitted set exit 2. But `engine.roleUnits` (internal/engine/nextunits.go:237-251) derives units from ResolveActiveCorpus minus DropDisabledRoles — it filters on `disabled-by-spec` and on nothing else. Emission skips roles for four further reasons (internal/engine/skipped.go:28-32: `no-checklist-items`, `no-spec-change`, `domain-mismatch`, `no-baseline`), and `no-checklist-items` is decided at emission time inside generateRoleAuditPrompts (internal/cli/audit_roles.go:334-336), which roleUnits never runs. So the driver spawns an audit-role unit for a corpus role whose checklist came back empty; today that unit runs `tp audit <spec>`, gets exit 0 and a panel, and after this release it runs `tp audit <spec> --role <id>` and gets exit 2 with no prompt at all. §4.2 spends six bullets on the flag's refusal surface and never states what the driver must do when the id it spawned is not in the set the same round emits.
suggestion: Rule it explicitly in §4.2: either (a) `--role <id>` for a name that is in the active corpus but skipped at this emission exits 0 with an empty `prompts[]` and the role's `skipped_roles` entry, so the unit can stop cleanly rather than fail on its brief; or (b) make roleUnits derive the unit set from the same skip evaluation emission uses, so no unit is ever spawned for a skipped role. Whichever is chosen, add a test to §6.4 that spawns a round with a `no-checklist-items` skip and asserts the unit's own brief command's exit code.

finding: §4.2's brief change makes a unit's own brief command fail for a role the same round legitimately does not emit, because the unit set and the emitted role set are derived by two different filters and §4.2 assumes they are equal. Verified in the tree: engine.roleUnits (internal/engine/nextunits.go:237) builds one unit per role from ResolveActiveCorpus + ResolveOverrideFocus + DropDisabledRoles — i.e. domain filtering and enabled:false only. The other three skip reasons in engine/skipped.go are applied LATER, at emission: no-checklist-items is decided in internal/cli/audit_roles.go:334 from the per-role file selection (`items = fileCheckItems(sel.CodeFiles, role.ID)`; empty selection => role skipped), and no-spec-change is decided at emission under --diff-from. So an audit round whose git diff selects no code files still spawns an audit-role unit for every corpus code role, while `tp audit <spec>` emits no prompt for any of them. Under the old brief that unit received the panel, found nothing for itself and exited 0. Under §4.2's brief it runs `tp audit <spec> --role <id>`, the id is outside 'the set this same invocation would emit', and §4.2 bullet 3 makes that exit 2 — a failed unit, and under `tp run` a stopped round. §4.4 and test 14 pin only the opposite direction (a role emitted with no unit, i.e. regression); the direction that is now fatal is unpinned and unmentioned.
suggestion: State the invariant in the direction that now matters: every unit the driver spawns must have a prompt in the emission its brief performs. Either (a) make roleUnits apply the same skip predicates the emitter applies, so no unit is created for a role that will be skipped — this is the honest fix and it also makes test 14's set comparison total; or (b) carve out an exit-0 no-op: `--role <name>` for a name the invocation SKIPPED (as opposed to never knew) emits an empty prompts[] with the skipped_roles entry and exits 0, so a unit with nothing to do reports that rather than failing. Add a test that runs an audit round with an empty code-file selection end-to-end through `tp run --dry-run` and asserts the spawned units' brief commands all exit 0.

finding: §2.3's construction and §1/§6.2-test-5/§7-criterion-1's figure differ by exactly one byte, and the figure is asserted as an exact integer, so an implementer who builds §2.3 fails the release's own gate. §2.3 emits `<the body as v0.35.2 emits it, with any trailing newline removed>` + LF LF + §2.2's clause + LF LF + §3.2's clause, `and no trailing newline`. Measured on the shipped binary (`tp review spec/0.36.0.md --round 4 --json`, TP_* cleared): all five emitted prompts today end with a trailing newline — every one tails `content above is complete and authoritative.\n`. So the delta §2.3 constructs is -1 (the removed newline) + 2 + 287 + 2 + 177 = 467 bytes, not 468. Clause bytes verified independently: §2.2's line is 287 bytes, §3.2's is 177. §6.2 test 5 says `exactly 468 bytes longer ... asserted as an exact integer`, and §7 criterion 1 says the per-role diff must be `the 468 bytes §2.3 appends` and that `a difference anywhere else fails the gate`. The release therefore cannot pass its own gate as specified.
suggestion: Pick one and make all four sites agree. Either keep the existing trailing newline (append LF LF + clause + LF LF + clause after it and let the body still end with no newline, restating the delta as 468 only if the arithmetic actually yields it), or keep §2.3's construction and change §1, §6.2 test 5 and §7 criterion 1 to 467 with the -1 shown in the arithmetic. §2.3's sentence `That is 4 separator bytes, which is the figure §1 prices and test 5 asserts` should state the net delta, not the separator count, since the separator count is not the number the test asserts.

finding: §3.1 diagnoses a deferral to a spec that does not own the question, states the lesson ('Naming an owner that does not own it is worse than naming none'), and then commits the same error against the replacement target without checking it. §3.1 says: 'Earlier drafts routed it to spec/0.41.0.md §2; checked against that file, §2 is Sharding a role's checklist ... It belongs in spec/0.38.0.md, the backlog release.' Verified against spec/0.38.0.md as it stands: 97 lines, nine sections — Overview, Determinism and shape of agent-facing output, `done --batch` input contract, Sub-mode precedence, Warning channel, Resolve safety, Evidence-line counting, Non-Goals, Tests. The strings 'partial', 'unit', 'complete', 'promote', 'promoteRoleFindings' and 'regression' do not occur in it at all. So the file named as the owner of 'whether a partial file should ever complete a unit' contains no unit-lifecycle surface whatsoever. The same unchecked move is made a second time: §4.4 and Non-Goal 6 route the regression-unit repair to spec/0.38.0.md ('squarely spec/0.38.0.md's kind of item'), and that file likewise never mentions the panel, the driver or the role. Two open questions this release deliberately leaves open are therefore both parked with a non-owner, which is exactly the state §3.1 says is worse than parking them nowhere.
suggestion: Apply §3.1's own check to the replacement. Either add the two questions to spec/0.38.0.md as sections (a completeness predicate for a partial role findings file; a unit for the regression role) and cite those section numbers from §3.1, §3.3, §4.4, Non-Goal 5 and Non-Goal 6 — or state, in each of those five places, that the question is UNOWNED and record it in spec/0.35.0-candidates.md, which is this repository's documented home for a deferral with a reason. A routing that names a file must name a section in it.

finding: `prompts[]` entries are not independent of each other, so `reduced to the single entry whose role equals <name>` is order-sensitive and §4.2 never says whether the reduction happens before or after prompt assembly. The emitter has a position-dependent inliner: internal/cli/review.go:940-963 and internal/cli/audit_roles.go:315-370 give the affected files' whole contents to the FIRST emitted role whose set fits the per-role budget (`inlinerDone`, `set once, never reset`) and give every later role named paths only. Two orders, two different artifacts: filter-before-assembly makes the selected role the inliner, so its prompt is no longer byte-identical to its entry in the unrestricted invocation and §6 test 6 fails; filter-after-assembly satisfies test 6 but hands three of four units a prompt that no longer has the file bodies any unit could previously read out of the panel. `tp audit` auto-detects affected files from git diff, so this is the live case, not a hypothetical one. §7 criterion 1 compares per-role bytes and by construction cannot see it: each role's own prompt is unchanged; what disappears is the cross-role content the panel used to carry. That is precisely the suppression shape §7 exists to catch.
suggestion: State the order in §4.2 (`prompts are assembled in full and then filtered`, so the selected entry is byte-identical), and add to §4.4 that a non-inliner role selected with --role receives named paths only — with the consequence named, since under `tp run` that is a real content reduction, not just a byte reduction. Add a §6.3 test that runs a multi-role emission with --affected-files and asserts the non-inliner role's --role prompt equals its unrestricted entry AND does not contain the file bodies, so the loss is pinned rather than discovered.

finding: §4.2 claims `Three distinct operator mistakes, three distinct hints` but rules on one of the five reasons a role can be absent from the emitted set, leaving the implementer to invent the other four. internal/engine/skipped.go:28-32 defines `no-checklist-items`, `no-spec-change`, `domain-mismatch`, `no-baseline`, `disabled-by-spec`. Bullet 4 covers only `disabled-by-spec` (`the per-spec deactivation of v0.32.0`). For the other four the name is in the active corpus and absent from `prompts[]`, which is the same observable, so an implementer must decide whether each gets the `skipped` hint of bullet 4 or the unknown-name hint of bullet 3 — and §6 test 9 pins only one token, `skipped`, for one of them. §6 test 7 exercises `no-baseline` directly (`At round 1, where regression is skipped no-baseline, the same command exits 2`) and asserts only the exit code, so the spec's one worked example of a non-`disabled-by-spec` skip is silent on the hint it is supposed to demonstrate. Precedence is also unstated: a name can be skipped for this spec AND active in the other phase's corpus, and §4.2 gives no rule for which of its two hints wins.
suggestion: Replace bullet 4 with a rule keyed on `skipped_roles[].reason` rather than on one reason: any name that appears in this invocation's `skipped_roles` exits 2 with a hint that names the reason verbatim; a name in neither `prompts[]` nor `skipped_roles` but present in the other phase's corpus gets the cross-phase hint; anything else is unknown. State the precedence explicitly (skipped > cross-phase > unknown), and extend §6 test 9 to cover one case per reason so the five-way surface is pinned rather than the one-way surface.

finding: §4.2 states a rule and violates it in the adjacent cell of the same table. It moves --verify to the refused column with the reason: 'it already emits exactly one prompt (role `verifier`); --role there could only be a no-op or a refusal, and a flag that cannot change the output should not be accepted.' But --perspective is in the LEGAL column, and every one of its four values also emits exactly one prompt. Measured on the shipped binary against this spec: `--perspective documentation` 1 prompt, `--perspective testing` 1, `--perspective code-audit` 1, `--perspective regression` 1 — all four with an empty output_path, exactly like --verify's. So the stated principle condemns --perspective on identical evidence, and §6.3 test 11 then requires the accepted behaviour ('--role with --perspective ... exits 0 and emits one prompt'), pinning the violation. Either the principle is wrong or the table row is; the spec cannot hold both, and this matters because §4.2 is the only place the release explains why one adjacent flag is refused and another is not.
suggestion: Pick one and say why. If the principle stands, move --perspective to the refused column for `tp review` (leaving --diff-from as the only non-default legal mode) and delete test 11's --perspective case. If --perspective stays legal, replace the --verify reason with the real discriminator — e.g. `verifier` is not a corpus role and carries no output_path, so it is not a member of any panel --role can index — and state explicitly that a --role that names the one prompt a single-prompt mode emits is accepted as a no-op.

finding: §4.2's 'three distinct operator mistakes, three distinct hints' taxonomy is built on a reading of `skipped_roles` that tp's own contract contradicts. §4.2 bullet 4 says 'A name in the corpus but in `skipped_roles` for this spec (the per-spec deactivation of v0.32.0)' — equating the key with one reason. `skipped_roles` carries FIVE reasons (internal/engine/skipped.go: no-checklist-items, no-spec-change, domain-mismatch, no-baseline, disabled-by-spec; contract in spec/0.29.0.md §9.1, restated in skills/tp/REFERENCE.md). Two consequences the spec does not cover. (1) `regression` at round 1 IS in skipped_roles with reason no-baseline (spec/0.29.0.md §10.3; asserted by TestReviewSkippedRoles_RegressionNoBaseline in internal/cli/role_attribution_transparency_test.go), yet it is NOT 'in the corpus' — §4.1 itself says ParseRoleBytes refuses it as a corpus file. So bullet 4's conjunction excludes it, it falls to bullet 3, and §6.3 test 7's round-1 refusal returns the *unknown-role* hint for a role the same payload reports as skipped with a reason. (2) A corpus role skipped for domain-mismatch, no-spec-change or no-checklist-items lands in bullet 4 and gets a hint saying only 'skipped', suppressing the reason tp already computed — and no-spec-change is reachable from a mode §4.2 legalises (--diff-from).
suggestion: Key the hint on the data instead of on corpus membership: if `<name>` appears in this invocation's `skipped_roles`, refuse with a hint that names the role AND its reason verbatim (one branch, five reasons, no enumeration to drift); if it is active in the other phase's corpus, name that phase; otherwise list the emitted names. Restate §6.3 test 9 as three refusals matched on the reason token (`no-baseline`, `disabled-by-spec`, `domain-mismatch`) plus the cross-phase and unknown cases, and make test 7's round-1 assertion require the `no-baseline` token rather than only exit 2.

finding: Test 5 asserts an exact integer that a correct implementation of §2.3 cannot produce, and test 12 describes a diff that §2.3 contradicts. §2.3's construction is '<the body as v0.35.2 emits it, with any trailing newline removed> LF LF <§2.2 clause> LF LF <§3.2 clause>' and no trailing newline. Measured on the shipped binary (round-4 emission, TP_* cleared): every prompts[].prompt ends with exactly one 0x0A. So the net delta is -1 (stripped LF) + 2 + 287 + 2 + 177 = +467 bytes, not the 468 that §1 prices, §2.3 asserts ('That is 4 separator bytes, which is the figure §1 prices and test 5 asserts'), test 5 pins 'as an exact integer', and §7 criterion 1 exempts as 'the 468 bytes §2.3 appends'. Independently, test 12's 'differs from the v0.35.2 baseline only by the two clauses inside each prompts[].prompt' is false under §2.3: a byte is also REMOVED from each role prompt, so a strict diff shows a deletion the test says will not be there. Two engineers also split on 'any trailing newline': TrimSuffix(body,"\n") removes one and TrimRight(body,"\n") removes all, which changes the delta again if the body ever ends with more than one LF.
suggestion: Pick one and make all four sites agree. Either (a) keep the strip and restate the figure as 467 everywhere (§1 'What it costs', §2.3's closing sentence, test 5, §7 criterion 1), and reword test 12 as 'differs only by the removal of the body's trailing newline and the two appended clauses'; or (b) drop the strip — append LF+clause+LF+LF+clause to the body as emitted — and keep 468. Either way replace 'any trailing newline removed' with the exact operation ('remove exactly one trailing LF if present' vs 'remove all trailing LFs'), since the two are distinguishable and test 5 is an exact-integer assertion.

finding: Test 7 asserts only 'the same command exits 2' for `--role regression` at round 1 and does not pin the hint, while §4.2 routes that exact case two contradictory ways. §4.1 calls the round-1 state 'skipped with reason `no-baseline`', which reads onto §4.2 bullet 4 ('A name in the corpus but in `skipped_roles` for this spec ... exits 2 with a hint that says it is *skipped*, not unknown'). But verified on the shipped binary, the emitted `skipped_roles` key is `[]` at round 1 — regression is not a member of it, and §4.2 bullet 4 also scopes itself to names 'in the corpus', which §4.1 says regression can never be ('engine.ParseRoleBytes refuses it as a corpus file'). Under bullet 3 the same command produces the unknown-name hint listing the four emitted roles. So one engineer asserts a hint containing 'skipped' and another asserts a hint listing architect/ax-economist/implementer/tester, and both can cite the spec. Test 9 pins tokens for three refusals and this fourth, constructible case is not one of them.
suggestion: State in §4.2 which of the three hints a role that is emittable-but-not-emitted-this-round (regression skipped `no-baseline`) receives, and why. Then extend test 7 with the required token for that hint, or add it to test 9's list as a fourth pinned case. If the answer is 'the unknown-name hint', say so explicitly in §4.1 so the word 'skipped' there is not read as a reference to `skipped_roles`.

finding: §6.1 and §7 give two incompatible acquisition methods for the same baseline, so the two comparisons cannot share a harness. §6.1 says the v0.35.2 payload 'is obtained by running the v0.35.2 emitter in-process against the same fixture — the release tag is in this repository'. Verified: HEAD is at v0.35.2 and v0.36.0 replaces that emitter in the same package, so once the release is implemented no in-process call can reach the old emitter; only an out-of-process build from the tag (git worktree + go build) or a vendored copy of the old emitter can. §7 in fact says the opposite — 'compare against the same emission from the v0.35.2 binary'. The tag is evidence for the binary route and against the in-process one, and §6.1 cites it while asserting the in-process one. Two engineers write incompatible fixtures: one copies buildReviewPrompts into testdata and calls it, the other builds the tag and shells out; their byte results differ if anything outside the emitter (corpus loading, state reading) also changed.
suggestion: Name one method in §6.1 and have §7 cite it rather than restate it. The binary route is the only one both sections can share: state that the test builds `tp` at tag v0.35.2 into t.TempDir() once (TestMain or a sync.Once helper), runs it with the fixture and captures stdout, and that §7's replay uses that same helper. If the in-process route is preferred, say explicitly which package the v0.35.2 emitter is vendored into and that it is frozen.

finding: §6.1 exists to fix the baseline that tests 5 and 12 compare against, and it names two mutually exclusive mechanisms in adjacent sentences — with §7 supplying a third phrasing. Sentence 1: the baseline 'is obtained by running the v0.35.2 emitter IN-PROCESS against the same fixture'. In-process means the v0.35.2 emitter is linked into the v0.36.0 test binary, i.e. a second copy of the emitter is committed to this tree — which the sentence that follows ('Nothing is committed') denies, and which the project quality gate acts against twice: `deadcode` reports a function reachable only from tests, and `dupl` (enabled, 150-token default) fires on a near-clone of the live emitter. Sentence 2 gives a different mechanism: 'the release TAG is in this repository, so the test builds the baseline rather than storing it' — building a git ref is inherently out-of-process (checkout + compile), and a `go test` that shells out to build another revision is a materially different cost and a different failure mode than an in-process call. §7 then says 'compare against the same emission from the v0.35.2 BINARY', which matches sentence 2 and not sentence 1. Two tests and a release gate depend on this being one procedure.
suggestion: Choose the out-of-process form and write it as steps, since it is the only one compatible with 'nothing is committed': the test (or the gate script) runs `go build` at tag v0.35.2 into a temp dir once per run, invokes that binary with the fixture spec and the explicitly fixed inputs §6.1 already lists (round number, loop budget, consecutive-clean count, output_path), and diffs its stdout against the v0.36.0 binary's. Say where the build is cached, what happens when the tag is absent (skip with a named reason, or fail), and delete 'in-process'. Then align §7's wording to the same sentence rather than paraphrasing it.

finding: §6.1 makes four inputs load-bearing and then leaves the pinning mechanism to the implementer with one sentence: 'Each test fixes those inputs explicitly.' The inputs are the round number, the loop budget, the consecutive-clean count and the output_path — none of which is a parameter of `tp review`. Measured against the shipped binary, tp exposes exactly two seams: `--round N` and `--no-state`. `--no-state` fixes all four (it emits round 1, previous_findings 0, round-relative output_path) but it also forces round 1, which suppresses the `regression` role entirely — verified: `tp review spec/0.36.0.md --no-state` emits 4 prompts, no regression, `review_loop.round == 1`. So the one flag that pins the inputs disables the round-dependence §4.1 exists to establish and makes test 7's positive case ('--role regression succeeds at a round where regression is emitted') unreachable from the same fixture. This project has already been burned by exactly this shape once, with --no-state switching off the machine under measurement. Nothing in §6.1 warns of it, and no seam at all is named for the loop budget or the consecutive-clean count.
suggestion: Say per input how it is fixed, and say which fixture each of tests 5, 7 and 12 uses. Concretely: the tests that need a round >= 2 panel (7, 12, and the emitted-set definition of test 6) must construct a review-state directory on disk under a t.TempDir() spec base — a snapshot-round-(N-1).md plus a review-round-(N-1).ndjson — rather than use --no-state; the tests that only need any single role prompt (1-5) may use --no-state and should say so. Add an explicit warning that --no-state is not usable for any test whose subject is the round-dependent panel.

finding: §6.1 specifies the baseline for tests 5 and 12 as `running the v0.35.2 emitter in-process against the same fixture`, and that is not something a Go test in this module can do. A `go test` binary compiles one source tree — the current one; v0.35.2's `buildReviewPrompts` and `generateRoleAuditPrompts` are unexported functions of `internal/cli` at a tag, not an importable package, and adding them as a self-import is a module cycle. §6.1 then closes the two remaining doors: a stored blob is explicitly refused (`Nothing is committed`), and the only other route — check out the tag into a temp worktree, `go build`, exec the binary — is out-of-process, needs git and a Go toolchain during `go test -race ./...` (the project gate, which CI runs), and contradicts the section's own word `in-process`. §6.1's last sentence, `Each test fixes those inputs explicitly`, also names no mechanism: `--round` is a flag, but required-clean and consecutive-clean come from workflow config and review state, which a built v0.35.2 binary reads from the repo rather than from arguments.
suggestion: Name the actual mechanism and make it one an implementer can run under the project gate. The buildable options are: (a) vendor the v0.35.2 body-assembly function into a `_test.go` file as a frozen literal helper, so `in-process` is true and nothing is committed as data; or (b) drop `in-process`, state that the baseline is a binary built from the tag in a temp worktree, mark tests 5 and 12 as build-tagged/skipped when git or the toolchain is unavailable, and say so in §7 too since the gate needs the same binary. Also state how required-clean and consecutive-clean are pinned on the baseline side — probably `--no-state` plus an explicit `--round`, if that reproduces the framing block.

finding: Test 14's second clause cannot fail. 'Every role the round emits either has a unit or is absent from the units list' is a tautology over any pair of sets — a role either appears in the units list or does not — so an implementation that spawns zero units, or one that spawns units for the wrong roles, satisfies it. The sentence that follows ('The test asserts the two sets and their difference') does not say what the difference must equal, so `assert emitted - units == {"regression"}` and `assert len(emitted - units) >= 0` both satisfy §6.4, and only the first pins §4.4's claim that 'the loss stops being silent'. The first clause is also unpinned: 'has a brief naming a role' is satisfied by any non-empty string in the brief.
suggestion: Restate test 14 as two equalities against literal sets, both measurable from the same invocation: at a round where regression is emitted, `set(prompts[].role) - set(next_units[].id) == {"regression"}` and `set(next_units[].id) - set(prompts[].role) == {}`; at round 1 both differences are empty. That makes regression's absence a fact the test records and makes a driver that drops or adds a unit fail.

finding: The release's single most breaking failure mode has no test. §4.2 rests the whole saving on 'The mapping is exact and already exists' between a unit's id and the emitted role name; if the two ever diverge, every unit's brief hits §4.2's unknown-role rule, exits 2, and the round produces nothing at all. Verified today that they do match (tp resume emits unit ids architect/ax-economist/implementer/tester, which are exactly the emitted corpus role names), which is precisely why the invariant needs pinning before it silently breaks. Test 13 asserts only the brief's string SHAPE — that brief_command is `tp review <spec> --role <id>` with `<id>` the unit's own id — and test 14 asserts only that a brief 'names a role'. Neither executes the brief, so neither would catch an id that is not a member of the set that same invocation emits (for example a corpus role deactivated for the spec, or a future unit id that is not a role name).
suggestion: Add a test that closes the loop end to end: for every unit BuildNextUnits returns for a round, run its brief_command and assert exit 0 and exactly one prompts[] entry whose `role` equals the unit id. Assert it for both review-role and audit-role, and at a round >= 2 so the regression role is in the emitted set while absent from the unit set.

finding: Pass criterion 3 - the one §7 itself calls 'the part that would actually catch a suppression' - requires a `class` -> checklist-item mapping that does not exist and cannot be enumerated. `class` reaches a reviewer as an OPTIONAL free-text slug ('add "class":"<kebab-case-slug>" ... omit it otherwise'), so it is invented per finding rather than drawn from a registry. Measured over every `review-round-*.ndjson` under `spec/.tp-review/`: 2,772 recorded rows carry 2,178 distinct `class` values - 0.85 distinct slugs per classed row, i.e. very nearly one vocabulary entry per finding - and 205 rows (7.4%) carry no `class` at all, so they cannot be mapped even in principle and §7 gives them no rule. This is CLAUDE.md's own measured pathology ('one idea arrived under 25 distinct class slugs') turned into a release gate. The cost is a ~2,178-entry hand-built artifact for a release §1 prices at 468 bytes, and the silent alternative is that the criterion passes vacuously.
suggestion: Drop the class indirection and check the property directly on the artifacts §7 already builds, which is where the suppression risk actually lives: for each replayed round and each role, assert the set of checklist items in the v0.36.0 `--role <r>` prompt is a superset of the set in the v0.35.2 panel entry for `r`. That needs no vocabulary, is mechanical, and covers the 205 class-less rows for free. If per-finding coverage is genuinely wanted, it first needs `class` to be a closed set - which is a different release.

finding: The release gate replays only review rounds, while half of what the release changes is `tp audit` emission — and §7's own anti-silence clause cannot catch the omission. §7 enumerates 'each recorded round R of each spec under `spec/.tp-review/` that has a `snapshot-round-R.md` and a `review-round-R.ndjson`'. Verified on disk: audit state in that same directory is named `audit-round-R.ndjson` and `snapshot-audit-round-R.md` (spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/ holds 9 audit rounds and 21 review rounds under exactly those two naming schemes). So zero audit rounds are replayed. Yet §2.2 spends a paragraph choosing the clause's wording specifically so it is correct in `tp audit` prompts ('a clause that said the findings file would be wrong in half the prompts it is emitted into'), §4.2's mode table gives `tp audit` its own row, and §6.3 test 6 says '`tp audit` likewise'. §7's closing safeguard — 'A round whose snapshot or findings file is missing is reported as un-replayable and named, never silently skipped' — does not fire, because those rounds are not missing artifacts; they are outside the enumeration. The gate that exists because this release narrows what a reviewer sees is blind to the phase where §4.4's acknowledged panel/unit divergence actually bites (see the §4.2 unit-brief finding).
suggestion: Make the enumeration cover both phases: for each spec under `spec/.tp-review/`, replay every round R that has (`snapshot-round-R.md`, `review-round-R.ndjson`) through `tp review` and every round R that has (`snapshot-audit-round-R.md`, `audit-round-R.ndjson`) through `tp audit`, applying all three pass criteria to each. State the audit-side adaptation of criterion 3 explicitly, since an audit row is keyed by (role, item_id) and carries a status rather than a class.

finding: §7's criterion 3 — the part §7 itself calls 'the part that would actually catch a suppression' — rests on a `class` -> checklist-item mapping that does not exist anywhere in tp, and the spec introduces none. It says: 'For each recorded finding in `review-round-R.ndjson`, the role that produced it still receives a prompt containing the checklist item its `class` maps to.' Verified against this spec's own recorded rounds: a stored finding's keys are exactly [category, class, finding, found_by, found_by_roles, location, role, severity, suggestion] — there is no checklist reference on the row. And `class` is not a controlled vocabulary: the emitted output contract marks it optional ('add "class" ... when the finding is an instance of a pattern a script could check; omit it otherwise') and reviewers coin it freely — round 3 of this spec has 40 distinct classes across 41 rows, round 1-3 together 140 (location,class) pairs of which essentially every class is unique. There is no total function from a per-finding slug to a checklist item, so criterion 3 has no evaluable predicate, which is the same defect §7 was rewritten to remove from criteria 1 and 2. Non-Goal 7 ('the checklist items ... are untouched') also forecloses adding a class field to the checklist as part of this release.
suggestion: Replace the class-based criterion with one computable from what tp already stores. The recorded finding carries `role` and `location`; the prompt carries the role's numbered checklist. So assert instead: for every (role, location) pair in `review-round-R.ndjson`, the v0.36.0 `--role <role>` prompt for round R contains the same checklist item set as the v0.35.2 prompt for that role — i.e. criterion 3 becomes 'no checklist item is lost for any role that produced a finding', which is a set comparison over text tp emits, not a mapping tp does not have. If a class-level guarantee is genuinely wanted, it needs a class taxonomy, and that is a different release.

finding: §7's replay reads `snapshot-round-R.md` as if it were the spec round R reviewed, and for 19% of this repository's recorded rounds it demonstrably is not. Measured just now across `spec/.tp-review/`: 221 recorded rounds in 15 specs, 201 of them with a snapshot file, and for 38 of those 201 the snapshot's sha256 does not equal the `spec_hash` that `state.json` recorded for the same round (0.31.0 rounds 2-20, 0.32.0 rounds 6-12, 0.24.0 rounds 1-4, 0.35.0 review 4 and 10 plus audit 5-7, 0.31.2 rounds 2-3, 0.29.0 round 1). The cause is stated in this spec's own §2.2: any `tp review <spec>` rewrites the current round's snapshot from the spec on disk, and §2.2 explicitly licenses every unit to run it - verified here, this unit's own measurement invocation rewrote `snapshot-round-4.md` at 14:10:15. §7's failure protocol covers only a MISSING snapshot ('reported as un-replayable and named'); a stale one is silent. So on 19% of its scope the gate diffs prompts built from text no reviewer ever saw and reports a pass.
suggestion: `state.json` already stores the discriminator. Add to §7: before replaying round R, verify sha256(snapshot-round-R.md) equals that round's recorded `spec_hash`, and classify a mismatch exactly as §7 already classifies a missing file - un-replayable and named, never silently replayed. Report three counts in the gate artifact (replayed, missing, hash-mismatched) so a shrinking replayable set cannot be read as a passing gate.

finding: §7's third pass criterion has no implementable predicate, and it is the one §7 itself calls load-bearing: `This is the part that would actually catch a suppression`. It requires that for each recorded finding, `the role that produced it still receives a prompt containing the checklist item its class maps to`. No class-to-checklist mapping exists anywhere in tp and this spec does not define one. `class` is a free-form kebab-case slug the reviewer invents at write time — the emitted prompt says `add "class":"<kebab-case-slug>" ... when the finding is an instance of a pattern a script could check`, with no enumeration and no registry; the engine's only uses of the field are clustering and mechanize-candidate counting (internal/engine/mechanized.go, cluster.go), none of which relates a class to a checklist item. Checklist items, meanwhile, are generated per emission from the spec's structured elements and renumber whenever the spec's tables and lists change, so even a hand-written mapping would not survive between the round being replayed and the replay. An implementer cannot write this check.
suggestion: Replace criterion 3 with something derivable from what tp records. The recorded row already carries `location` and `role`; a runnable form is: for each recorded finding, the v0.36.0 `--role <its role>` prompt for that round still contains the checklist item covering its `location` section — matched on the section anchor tp already dedups by — and the count of checklist items per role is unchanged from v0.35.2. If the class-level claim is wanted, §7 must first define where the class-to-checklist mapping lives and who writes it, which is new surface and probably belongs to spec/0.40.0.md.

finding: §2.3 states an emission predicate for the CLAUSES ('appended to every prompt whose output_path is non-empty, and to no other') but none for the trailing-newline STRIP that the same construction performs. Two readings are both consistent with §2.3 and neither is excluded by any test: (a) the body is trimmed only when the clauses are appended, so a prompt with an empty output_path still ends with the LF it ends with today; (b) the body is trimmed for every prompt and the clauses appended for some, so the test-planner and verifier prompts also lose their trailing newline. Test 4 asserts only that the clauses are absent, so both implementations pass it, while test 12's byte-diff against the v0.35.2 payload comes out differently under the two (one deletion per role prompt vs one per prompt).
suggestion: Say that the strip is part of the append and happens only when the clauses are emitted. Then strengthen test 4 to assert that a prompt with an empty output_path is byte-identical to the v0.35.2 prompt for the same mode, which pins the negative for the newline as well as for the clauses and is the same baseline test 12 already builds.

finding: §4.2's second half changes `UnitKind.BriefCommand` for `review-role` and `audit-role`, and buys test 13 plus an end-to-end `tp run --dry-run` assertion, in order to hand the child a value the child already holds. `internal/engine/childenv.go` sets `TP_UNIT_ID` to exactly the `<id>` §4.2 appends to the brief, and the emitter already reads the sibling variable for precisely this purpose: `roleOutputPath` (internal/cli/prompt_framing.go:44) branches on `engine.EnvRoundDir` to choose the role's output path, which §2.2 cites as established behaviour. Defaulting `--role` from `TP_UNIT_ID` when it is set adds no surface, leaves `spec/0.35.0.md` §3.3.1's fixed brief contract alone, and delivers the 90.6% to every already-issued brief and to the shipped agent definitions without any of them changing. §4.5 rejects `prompt_path` on exactly this test - 'carries no information its consumer lacks' - and §4.2 neither applies it to itself nor records that the cheaper option was considered.
suggestion: Keep `--role`: the interactive path has no `TP_UNIT_ID` and genuinely needs the flag. Then pick one and say which. Either (a) the flag defaults to `TP_UNIT_ID` under a run, and the brief change plus test 13 are deleted; or (b) the brief change stays and §4.2 gains one sentence pricing the alternative and saying why explicitness wins - this repo's documented de-magic preference is a real argument, it is simply not made. As it stands the more expensive of the two ships with no record that the other was seen.

finding: §4.4 books a benefit - 'What this release does change is that the loss stops being silent' - that no emitted artifact delivers. Today `regression`'s prompt appears in every unit's `prompts[]` (measured on this round: 89,420 of 171,955 prompt bytes). After §4.2's brief it appears in none, and nothing is emitted in its place: `--role` narrows `prompts[]` and adds no key naming what was dropped, and the payload's existing precedent for exactly this reporting job - `skipped_roles`, which names a role the caller does not get and is `[]` this round - is not extended. The only place the fact is recorded is §6 test 14, which runs in CI, not during a cycle. So a driver or operator reading a round's output after this release sees strictly LESS about `regression` than before it. §4.1's own word for the current state is 'buried'; the release replaces burial with absence and calls the difference visibility.
suggestion: Pick one. Either drop the sentence and let Non-Goal 6 carry the defect alone - it already states it honestly, and test 14 is a fine regression pin with no benefit claim attached - or make it observable for the cost of one key: report roles the invocation emitted but assigned to no unit, the way `skipped_roles` already reports roles it did not emit, and have test 14 assert that key instead of a set difference computed inside the test.

finding: Test 10's discriminating instruction cannot be followed for three of the seven refusing review modes. It says each case is 'run with the refusing mode's *own* arguments absent', which 'is what makes the test discriminating'. Verified against `tp review --help`: `--record` is a string flag, so it cannot be supplied with its argument absent — omitting the value is a cobra parse error before any tp code runs, and supplying one makes the test's property depend on which value (a nonexistent path exits on the file check, an existing one does not), which the spec never states. `--merge`, `--resolve` and `--resolve-all` take their input as the POSITIONAL, which is the same argv slot the spec path occupies, so 'arguments absent' is undefined there too: dropping the positional also drops the spec, and the hint the test wants ('naming both flags') then competes with a missing-spec error. Two engineers write different argv and get different exit paths.
suggestion: Give the exact argv per row of §4.2's table rather than a rule. For `--record`, specify a path that does not exist, so the ordering property is genuinely discriminating (the flag-conflict error must beat the file error). For `--merge`/`--resolve`/`--resolve-all`, say whether the spec positional is present and what the second positional is, since those modes reinterpret the positional slot.

finding: Test 4's enumeration is not runnable as written. It asserts the negative over 'every mode that emits such a prompt: --perspective testing (role test-planner), --perspective documentation, --perspective code-audit, and --verify (role verifier)', but three of the four refuse to emit anything without an extra required argument the test never names. Verified on the shipped binary: `--perspective testing` exits 2 with '--test-path is required when --perspective=testing'; `--perspective documentation` exits 2 with '--docs-path is required'; `--perspective code-audit` exits 2 with 'requires at least one --affected-files'; `--verify` exits 2 with '--verify requires --findings'. Only `--perspective testing --test-path <dir>` was confirmed to actually emit a prompt with output_path == "". Two of the four modes also have no role named, so a writer cannot tell whether they emit one prompt or several, nor what to assert if a mode ever emits a mixed set.
suggestion: For each of the four rows give the extra argument the mode needs and the role(s) it emits, so the enumeration is a runnable table. Then state the assertion over the payload rather than per mode: for every prompts[] entry in every listed invocation, output_path == "" implies neither clause string occurs in prompt — which stays correct even if a mode later emits more than one prompt.

finding: Test 4's enumeration of the modes that emit an empty-`output_path` prompt is missing one, and it is the one the test was designed to catch. §6.2 test 4 says `Asserted over every mode that emits such a prompt: --perspective testing (role test-planner), --perspective documentation, --perspective code-audit, and --verify (role verifier)`. §4.3 states `--perspective` has four values fixed in review.go, and the fourth is `regression`. Verified on the shipped binary: `tp review spec/0.36.0.md --perspective regression --round 4 --json` emits one prompt, role `regression`, `output_path` empty. The same role in the default panel carries a non-empty output_path (internal/cli/review.go:942-943 assigns one to every entry including regression), so `regression` is the single concrete instance of test 4's own stated rationale — `the discriminator is the empty output_path and not the role name, because the same role can carry a non-empty output_path in another mode` — and it is the one case the enumeration omits.
suggestion: Add `--perspective regression` to test 4's list and make it the worked case for the role-name-versus-output_path discriminator: assert that the same role `regression` gets the clauses in the default panel and does not get them under `--perspective regression`, in one test. That is the assertion that fails if an implementer keys the emission predicate on the role.

finding: §1's 'What it costs' prices this release at 468 bytes per prompt and nothing else, while §7 adds a release-blocking replay that is by far the larger cost and is neither priced nor scoped. As written - 'each recorded round R of each spec under `spec/.tp-review/`', 'once unrestricted and once per role', 'compare against the same emission from the v0.35.2 binary' - the scope on this repository today is 201 replayable rounds and, at the measured mean of 3.28 distinct roles per recorded round, about 1,900 emissions; one round-4 payload alone is 180,435 bytes. It also needs two artifacts nobody has: a runnable v0.35.2 emitter (§6.1 asks the tests to build one in-process, §7 assumes a binary, and the two are not the same thing) and a way to emit a past round's prompt with that round's number, previous findings and loop budget fixed - inputs the payload embeds and which `tp review <spec>` takes from live state, since no flag accepts them. And the artifact that records a pass is named as 'the per-round, per-role byte diffs', roughly 660 of them, with no summary form given.
suggestion: Scope it and price it in §1 beside the 468 bytes. A defensible scope is this spec's own rounds plus the most recent N rounds of each spec, stated as a number rather than 'each round of each spec'. Name the pass artifact as one summary line per round (roles compared, bytes differing, verdict) with full diffs retained only for failures. And say in §6.1 whether the v0.35.2 side is a vendored package, a `git worktree` build or a checked-in binary - the gate cannot be scheduled or budgeted until one is chosen.

finding: §7 applies criterion 3 to `each recorded round R of each spec under spec/.tp-review/`, and a tenth of that corpus does not carry the fields the criterion reads. Criterion 3 needs `role` (`the role that produced it`) and `class` on every recorded finding; both postdate the earlier rounds. Measured across every review-round-*.ndjson under spec/.tp-review/: 303 of 2772 recorded rows are missing `role` or `class` — 0.23.0 129 rows, 0.24.0 112, 0.25.0 59, 0.31.0 3 — and in 0.23.0 the figure is every row of every round (round 1: 64 rows, 0 with class, 0 with role). §7's only escape hatch is `A round whose snapshot or findings file is missing is reported as un-replayable and named`, which does not cover a round whose files are present but whose rows predate the schema. So the gate as written either fails on four of fifteen specs or silently skips them, which is the outcome the last sentence forbids.
suggestion: Add a third un-replayable case to §7's last paragraph: a round whose recorded rows lack the fields criterion 3 reads is reported as un-replayable-by-schema and named, alongside the missing-file case. State the cutoff explicitly (rows recorded before role/class were emitted) so the count is a fixed, reportable number rather than a per-run discovery, and decide whether criteria 1 and 2 — which need neither field — still run on those rounds.

finding: §7 says `re-emit the round's prompts from that snapshot` and names no invocation that can do it. A round-R role prompt embeds state that `snapshot-round-R.md` does not contain: the `## Changed sections since round R-1` block (which needs round R-1's snapshot), the previous-round findings summary and resolved-findings list (which needs `review-round-R-1.ndjson`), the round number, and the loop budget. §7's per-round precondition only requires `snapshot-round-R.md` and `review-round-R.ndjson`, so for R=1 of every spec there is no prior snapshot and for the first recorded round of a spec there is no prior findings file — yet §7 treats a round as replayable whenever its own two artifacts exist. No shipped flag reproduces a recorded round either: `--diff-from` takes a different prompt-builder path than the one the round used, and `--no-state` removes exactly the state the prompt embeds. Verified against the on-disk layout: spec/.tp-review/0.36.0/ holds snapshot-round-1..4.md and review-round-1..3.ndjson, so round 4 is a snapshot with no findings file and would be reported un-replayable, but round 1 has both artifacts and still cannot be re-emitted as it was.
suggestion: Write §7's replay as a concrete command line, including which artifacts feed which flag, and change the precondition to name every artifact the emission actually consumes (snapshot R, snapshot R-1, findings R-1, the round number, and the workflow's clean-round settings). If no existing flag combination reproduces a recorded emission, say so and scope the gate to the rounds that can be reproduced — or add the replay entry point as a task of this release rather than assuming one exists.
